title: Humanitarian crisis in the Sahel: scale, funding cuts, and paths to durable solutions
label: 20 October 2026 · The UK and the Sahel
summary: Witnesses described a regional crisis: some 20 million people displaced or uprooted across the Sahel and central Africa, driven by conflict, climate shocks and economic stress. They warned that sharp cuts in humanitarian and development funding are forcing life‑saving programmes to be cut, increasing food insecurity, protection risks and secondary displacement. The witnesses argued for coordinated action that combines humanitarian aid, long‑term development and climate finance, led by host governments, using better data and funding local organisations.

People forced to cross an international border because of conflict or persecution and who need protection.
United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the UN agency for refugees and displaced people.
World Food Programme, the UN agency that delivers food assistance and monitors food security.
A climate pattern that alters rainfall and temperatures, often causing droughts or floods that affect food production.

chapters.title: Scale and causes of the crisis
chapters.takeaway: The Sahel region faces a huge, long‑running displacement crisis driven by conflict, climate shocks and economic strain.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: Abdouraouf, can you set out the scale of humanitarian need across the Sahel?

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: About 20 million people are in forced displacement across west and central Africa: roughly 4 million refugees and 14 million IDPs, mostly in the central Sahel and neighbouring coastal states.

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: Eighty‑two percent are women and children, and average displacement lasts 15–20 years — so this is not short‑term relief work only.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: Where do you see this heading?

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: It depends on action now. If funding and coordination fail, more people will be forced to move further from their homes. We need humanitarian, development and private‑sector partners to work together.

turns.speaker: Marc Regnault de la Mothe
turns.text: On food, 9.7 million people face food insecurity in 2026 in the Sahel. Drivers include conflict, displacement, climate change and economic shocks. El Niño and global price rises will worsen food and fuel costs.

chapters.title: Funding cuts and frontline consequences
chapters.takeaway: Sharp reductions in humanitarian and development funding are forcing prioritisation, leaving millions without aid and increasing risks.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: You mentioned big funding cuts. What are the risks of leaving needs unmet?

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: Humanitarian funding fell about 50% in 2025 and ODA fell roughly 70% in some places. Cuts hit education, registration and protection, and prevent the investments needed for durable returns.

turns.speaker: Marc Regnault de la Mothe
turns.text: WFP has had to assist about 4 million fewer people than planned. We must prioritise, but that still leaves huge gaps; malnutrition and harmful coping strategies rise without funding.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can other organisations pick up the shortfall?

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: No—NGOs, local groups and UN agencies face the same cuts. We must coordinate closely to pool scarce resources and avoid duplicated short‑term responses.

turns.speaker: Marc Regnault de la Mothe
turns.text: Longer‑term resilience investments — land restoration, social protection and employment — reduce need over time, but they require predictable multi‑year funding.

chapters.title: Regional coordination and paths to durable solutions
chapters.takeaway: Sustainable solutions need government leadership, cross‑border cooperation, investment from development and climate finance, and local capacity building.

turns.speaker: Dr Sam Rushworth
turns.text: How does displacement across borders complicate UNHCR's work?

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: People move back and forth as IDPs, refugees or returnees. Return without jobs, schools or services causes repeat displacement. We use the Lomé dialogue to get states talking and sign tripartite protection agreements.

turns.speaker: Dr Sam Rushworth
turns.text: Patrice, how many Sudanese refugees is Chad hosting now?

turns.speaker: Patrice Ahouansou
turns.text: Sudanese refugees in Chad rose from about 400,000 to 1.3 million since April; total refugees including others are about 1.5 million. Chad has kept its borders open and is integrating refugees into national services.

turns.speaker: Patrice Ahouansou
turns.text: Refugees in Chad use Chadian schools and health centres; some live in camps, others in villages with host communities. Inclusion reduces tensions but needs extra investment and services funded by donors and development banks.

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: We’re pushing for development finance — World Bank and AfDB windows for host communities — so governments can invest in territories and make returns sustainable.

chapters.title: Access, diplomacy and non‑Western actors
chapters.takeaway: Humanitarian access is blocked by insecurity and government rules; coordinated diplomatic engagement helps, and new external actors are offering different financing options.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Vanessa, what blocks humanitarian access in the central Sahel?

turns.speaker: Vanessa Willems
turns.text: It varies by country: in Burkina Faso security incidents dominate; in Niger bureaucratic delays and permissions are the main problem; in Mali both apply. Examples: requiring aid cash be lodged in a treasury bank slowed purchases and payments.

turns.speaker: Vanessa Willems
turns.text: State claims of sovereignty are growing. That’s legitimate, but reforms need dialogue so restrictions don’t cripple response. Donors can help by coordinating diplomatic support and briefing embassies with field realities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are other states like China, Turkey or Russia influencing outcomes?

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: Some non‑Western actors are engaging differently — for example, private‑sector interest from China in development projects. States and governments seek diversified financing, so we’re convening private‑sector roundtables.

turns.speaker: Vanessa Willems
turns.text: Turkey sells drones to regional authorities; that raises protection risks. We ask external suppliers and partners to consider civilian protection when they sell military equipment.

turns.speaker: Yann Faivre
turns.text: Security and counter‑terror programmes need coordination with humanitarian actors. If stabilisation is uncoordinated, it can damage humanitarian neutrality and put aid workers at risk; sometimes sequencing or clearer risk‑sharing is needed.

chapters.title: Localisation, the Sahel Regional Fund and protection gaps
chapters.takeaway: The SRF shows that local leadership works, but funding cuts have reduced protection monitoring, GBV programmes and frontline capacity — hurting women, girls and other vulnerable groups the most.

turns.speaker: Dr Sam Rushworth
turns.text: How effective is the Sahel Regional Fund (SRF) at reaching local actors and enabling cross‑border work?

turns.speaker: Yann Faivre
turns.text: The SRF is efficient and trusted. It dedicates 25% directly to local partners and more via consortia, so roughly a third ends up delivered by local actors. It supports cross‑border responses and has low management costs.

turns.speaker: Vanessa Willems
turns.text: The SRF does more than money: it builds governance, pays indirect costs to local NGOs, supports NGO forums and funds innovation and mentoring. That makes localisation meaningful in practice.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: How have funding cuts affected programmes for women and girls?

turns.speaker: Yann Faivre
turns.text: GBV programmes have been hit hard; in some areas life‑saving protection services were cut and local women‑led organisations have closed. Those most vulnerable — women, girls, older people and people with disabilities — are worst affected.

turns.speaker: Vanessa Willems
turns.text: Protection monitoring has been seriously reduced: one year's data shows a quarter fewer organisations providing protection in the central Sahel between 2024 and 2025.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What data systems help you predict and target risks?

turns.speaker: Marc Regnault de la Mothe
turns.text: WFP uses the IPC food‑security system with FAO and governments to agree food needs and predict shocks; meteorological forecasting (Agrimet) helps predict El Niño impacts. Those systems need continued funding.

turns.speaker: Patrice Ahouansou
turns.text: UNHCR collects movement and impact data with communities, partners and governments. Integrating refugees and IDPs into national registries and social registries is key so government safety nets can reach them.

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: We have useful socioeconomic data shared with the World Bank, but there’s room to improve quality and coverage to underpin investment decisions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final thought: what should the UK do?

turns.speaker: Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde
turns.text: Continue funding life‑saving aid but also back pooled funds and development financing; use diplomatic influence to secure access; help link humanitarian programmes with World Bank and AfDB windows.

turns.speaker: Yann Faivre
turns.text: Support the SRF and predictable multi‑year funding, protect GBV and protection services, and sustain local partner financing.

turns.speaker: Vanessa Willems
turns.text: Use coordinated humanitarian diplomacy, brief embassies from field NGOs, and help create predictable, flexible funding that allows both short‑term response and multi‑year resilience investments.
